label: Bible Translations Compared
title: Six English Bibles, from word for word to thought for thought
intro: Every translation balances the form of the original against plain English. Each is placed here by how its own publisher describes its method.
image_title: Bible translations, from word for word to thought for thought
image_subtitle: Each placed by its publisher's own description of its method.
image_subtitle_narrow: Each placed by its publisher's own description of its method.
caption: Six widely read English Bibles on one line. Placement is approximate; the publishers describe their methods in words, not numbers.

positions.name: NASB
positions.text: Formal equivalence: word for word as much as possible, kept readable.
positions.short_text: Word for word as much as possible.

positions.name: ESV
positions.text: Essentially literal: as literal as possible, kept clear.
positions.short_text: As literal as possible, kept clear.

positions.name: CSB
positions.text: Optimal equivalence: both highly literal and highly readable.
positions.short_text: Aims to be both literal and readable.

positions.name: NIV
positions.text: Balances transparency to the original with clarity of meaning.
positions.short_text: Balances the original's form with clear meaning.

positions.name: NLT
positions.text: Meaning based: finds the meaning, then re-expresses it in English.
positions.short_text: Finds the meaning, then re-expresses it.

positions.name: The Message
positions.text: A reading Bible in the cadence of conversational English.
positions.short_text: A reading Bible in conversational English.

differ: Word for word Bibles keep the original's wording and sentence shape, which helps close study and can read stiffly.
Thought for thought Bibles carry the meaning into natural English, which reads easily and leans more on the translators' judgment.
The CSB and NIV each describe themselves as a balance between the two.
Crossway says every translation is at many points a trade-off between literal precision and readability.
voices_label: Each translation in its publisher's words
image_source: Sources: publisher statements from Lockman, Crossway, Lifeway, HarperCollins, Tyndale and NavPress
note: No translation is presented here as the only right choice.

sources.title: Lockman Foundation Family of Bible Translations
sources.quote: This method translates word-for-word from the original languages as much as possible.
sources.notes: On the NASB: 'it consistently uses the formal equivalence translation philosophy.' Also: 'it recognizes the need for the translation to be readable.'

sources.title: ESV Translation Philosophy
sources.quote: seeks as far as possible to reproduce the precise wording of the original text and the personal style of each Bible writer
sources.notes: Opens: the ESV is an 'essentially literal' translation; 'we have sought to be "as literal as possible" while maintaining clarity of expression and literary excellence.' Names the trade-off between 'formal equivalence' and 'functional equivalence'. The /translation/philosophy/ URL redirects here.

sources.title: CSB Translation Philosophy
sources.quote: Research shows the CSB is both highly literal to the original languages and highly readable, achieving an optimal blend of the two.
sources.notes: 'The CSB follows a translation philosophy called "optimal equivalence."' The site's publisher data names Lifeway.

sources.title: NIV Translation Philosophy
sources.quote: balancing transparency to the original with clarity of meaning
sources.notes: 'In 1965, the original NIV translation committee pioneered a different approach'. The page is (c) HarperCollins Publishers.

sources.title: What is Meaning-Based Translation?
sources.notes: 'In meaning-based translations, the translators start with a source-language text and dig beneath the surface to discover its meaning.' newlivingtranslation.com forwards to this site.

sources.title: What Is The Message?
sources.quote: The Message is a reading Bible translated from the original Greek and Hebrew Scriptures
sources.notes: Also: it 'combines the authority of God's Word with the cadence and energy of conversational English.' NavPress does not call it a paraphrase on this page, so this chart does not either.
